sections.heading: What EXIF Data Contains
paragraphs: EXIF is a standardized metadata format embedded in image files by cameras and phones, recording technical and contextual information alongside the pixel data.
Common fields include the camera manufacturer and model, lens information, exposure settings, ISO and focal length, plus a timestamp marking when the shot was taken.
On many devices, GPS coordinates are stored as well, along with the altitude and sometimes the compass direction the camera faced.
Even resized or edited exports can retain a surprising amount of this data, which is why a dedicated removal step is worth part of your sharing routine.

sections.heading: Removing Other Metadata for Complete Anonymity
paragraphs: Alongside EXIF, files may carry IPTC captions, XMP sidecar data and manufacturer extensions that hold names, copyright strings and editing histories.
A thorough cleanup removes these auxiliary metadata blocks too, not just the standard EXIF fields, so nothing incidental slips through.
Some platforms and messaging apps recompress photos and may add their own tags, making a final scrub before critical shares the safest habit.
Processing with a tool that clears the whole metadata envelope is the only reliable way to be certain the exported file is clean.

sections.heading: Everyday Situations That Call for EXIF Removal
paragraphs: Listing photos of your home or belongings for sale can reveal the exact location of your property, something buyers and strangers should not learn automatically.
Parents sharing photos of children on social media often prefer to strip location so that school playgrounds, homes and routines are not published to a wide audience.
Professionals like real estate agents, lawyers and delivery services send photos that may contain client-specific location data, which must be cleaned before forwarding.
Journalists and field workers operating in sensitive areas treat metadata removal as standard practice, because a single coordinate can endanger themselves or their sources.
